title: Distributed Systems: consensus with Raft
summary: Learn how a cluster of unreliable machines can agree on a single ordered log, using Raft as the worked example. You will move from replicated state machines and quorums through leader election, log replication and the commit rule, to snapshots, membership changes and linearizable clients, building a working Raft-backed key-value store along the way.

concepts.name: Replicated state machine
concepts.summary: Identical deterministic state machines that apply the same log of commands in the same order end up in the same state.

concepts.name: Consensus
concepts.summary: Getting a group of servers to agree on a sequence of values despite failures, with safety that never depends on timing.

concepts.name: Failure models
concepts.summary: The faults a protocol tolerates: crash-stop and crash-recover servers, lost or delayed messages and network partitions, but not Byzantine behaviour.

concepts.name: Majority quorum
concepts.summary: Any decision needs agreement from more than half the cluster, and any two majorities share at least one server.

concepts.name: Terms
concepts.summary: Monotonically increasing epochs that act as a logical clock, with at most one leader per term.

concepts.name: Server roles
concepts.summary: Every server is a follower, a candidate or the leader, and moves between these roles on timeouts and higher terms.

concepts.name: Raft RPCs
concepts.summary: RequestVote and AppendEntries are the only two RPCs basic Raft needs; InstallSnapshot is added for compaction.

concepts.name: Persistent state
concepts.summary: currentTerm, votedFor and the log must reach stable storage before a server answers an RPC; everything else can be rebuilt.

concepts.name: Leader election
concepts.summary: A follower that hears nothing for an election timeout becomes a candidate and wins the term with votes from a majority.

concepts.name: Randomized timeouts
concepts.summary: Spreading election timeouts over a range makes split votes rare and resolves them quickly.

concepts.name: Election restriction
concepts.summary: Voters refuse candidates whose log is less up-to-date than their own, so every new leader already holds all committed entries.

concepts.name: Log replication
concepts.summary: The leader pushes entries with AppendEntries, using a consistency check on the previous entry to force follower logs to match its own.

concepts.name: Commitment
concepts.summary: An entry is committed once the leader has stored an entry from its current term on a majority; committed entries are then applied in order.

concepts.name: Log compaction
concepts.summary: Snapshots replace a prefix of the log with the state it produced, and InstallSnapshot ships them to followers that fall behind.

concepts.name: Membership changes
concepts.summary: Changing the set of servers safely, one server at a time or via joint consensus, so two independent majorities never exist.

concepts.name: Client interaction
concepts.summary: Client sessions, duplicate detection and ReadIndex or leases turn Raft into a linearizable service.

modules.title: Foundations
modules.summary: Why replicated systems need consensus, which failures we design for, and the vocabulary Raft is built from: quorums, terms, roles and RPCs.

chapters.title: Terms, roles and the two RPCs

modules.title: Leader election
modules.summary: How a Raft cluster picks exactly one leader per term, recovers quickly from split votes, and makes sure the winner already holds every committed entry.

modules.title: Log replication
modules.summary: How the leader forces follower logs to match its own, and the precise rule that decides when an entry is committed and safe to apply.

modules.title: Operating Raft
modules.summary: What a production Raft needs beyond the core algorithm: bounded logs via snapshots, safe cluster reconfiguration, and exactly-once, linearizable client semantics.
